Council approves 14 km of protected cycle lanes along the river

By Hannah Okafor, transport reporter

22 October 2026
Share this story on social media Email this story to a friend

Riverside's city council voted 31 to 9 on Tuesday evening to build fourteen kilometres of protected cycle lanes along both banks of the river, the largest change to the city's streets in a generation.

The first section, between the old grain wharf and Station Bridge, is due to open next spring. Work on the remaining stretches will follow in three phases over the next four years, with the whole route finished by the summer of 2030.

Councillor Priya Raman, who chairs the transport committee, said the vote ended almost a decade of argument. "People have told us again and again that they would ride more if they felt safe doing it," she said. "This gives them a continuous route, kept apart from traffic, from one end of the city to the other."

The plan removes about 420 on-street parking spaces, most of them along Quay Street. To make up for part of the loss, the council will open the multi-storey car park on Mill Lane to overnight residents' permits at half the usual price.

Shop owners on Quay Street were divided. Tomasz Wieczorek, who runs a hardware shop near the market, said deliveries would become harder. "Our customers carry paint and timber. They are not going to do that on a bicycle," he said. Others welcomed the change: a baker two doors down said most of her morning trade already arrived on foot or by bike.

How the money breaks down

The scheme is expected to cost 38 million pounds. Just over half comes from a regional active travel fund, with the rest drawn from the council's own transport budget and from developer contributions linked to the new housing at the grain wharf.

Officers told the meeting that the lanes would be at least two metres wide in each direction and separated from the road by a raised kerb. At the eleven junctions along the route, cyclists will get their own signals, timed to give them a head start on turning traffic.

Opposition councillors argued that the money would be better spent on buses, which carry far more people each day. Councillor David Ashworth pointed out that the city's two busiest routes still run only every twenty minutes in the evening. The council leader replied that a review of the bus network would report in January.

A public consultation on the detailed design of the first phase opens next month and runs for six weeks. Drawings will be on display at the central library and at the community centre in Northgate.
